prompt: In replay.py, what is simulated and what is real?

choices.text: Everything is simulated, including the spans
choices.why: The spans are written by the real SDK as each request runs.

choices.text: The calendar and the people are simulated; every request runs for real
choices.why: Right. Spans carry the file's times, customers react by written rules, and every call is made and measured.

choices.text: The requests are real and the durations are invented
choices.why: The durations are measured; only the start times are shifted.

choices.text: Only the model is simulated
choices.why: The calendar and the customers' reactions are simulated too.

prompt: The traffic file had 284 requests. How many questions did the assistant receive during the replay?
The first trace of the week is a summary, and the customer's name is in its reply. Why did redaction not remove it?

choices.text: Redaction runs only on questions, never on replies
choices.why: Both app.question and app.reply go through redact().

choices.text: The summary feature skips redaction to keep summaries useful
choices.why: Every feature's text goes through the same function.

choices.text: The model invented the name, so it was not in the question
choices.why: It was in the conversation, and the model repeated it.

choices.text: Names have no shape that redact.py's patterns match
choices.why: Right. The order number went; the name stayed, in the question and in the reply.

prompt: Why does costs.py work out money when it reads the spans, instead of recording a cost on each span?

choices.text: Because spans cannot hold decimal numbers
choices.why: Spans hold floats and strings; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Because the provider forbids it
choices.why: No provider says anything about what goes on a span.

choices.text: Because prices change, and a cost written on a span cannot be corrected
choices.why: Right. Tokens are the fact; money depends on a price list that moves.

choices.text: Because computing a price would slow the reply down
choices.why: A multiplication costs nothing measurable.

prompt: What does an effective-dated price list do when a price changes?

choices.text: It adds a new row with a start date and keeps the old one for its days
choices.why: Right. Tuesday's cost has the same answer before and after the change.

choices.text: It overwrites the old price so reports use the new one
choices.why: That would change what last week cost, after the fact.

choices.text: It averages the old and the new price over the month in which the change happened
choices.why: No day was charged an average.

choices.text: It keeps only the price that was in force on the first day of the month
choices.why: Then a mid-month change would be charged wrongly for half the month.

prompt: At the price of llama3.2:3b before 30 September (2.00 input, 8.00 output, dollars per million), what do 1,000 input and 100 output tokens cost, in millionths of a dollar?
In the priced request, input was 90% of the tokens and 69% of the cost. What does that say about where to save?

choices.text: Shorter answers save the most, because output tokens cost four times as much
choices.why: Output is only 31% of this request's cost, however dear each token is.

choices.text: A shorter prompt saves more than a shorter answer
choices.why: Right. The prompt of sources and instructions is most of the bill.

choices.text: Nothing: the embedding dominates
choices.why: The embedding was 0.00000018 of 0.00081418.

choices.text: The cost is fixed per request
choices.why: It varies with how much is retrieved, as the spread showed.

prompt: The summaries were expected to be the most expensive feature and cost about what a help question does. Why?

choices.text: This week's conversations are short and the summaries are capped at forty words
choices.why: Right. The guess was about conversations in general; the measurement was about these.

choices.text: Summaries use a cheaper model
choices.why: They use llama3.2:3b like the rest.

choices.text: Summaries are cached
choices.why: Nothing in the assistant caches them.

choices.text: Staff requests are not billed
choices.why: Every call is billed, whoever makes it.

prompt: Why is the minimum cost of a help request zero, or nearly?

choices.text: Some help requests are free by contract
choices.why: There is no such contract.

choices.text: The model answers short questions for free, below a minimum number of tokens
choices.why: Every model call has input tokens and a price.

choices.text: The cost was rounded down to zero by costs.py
choices.why: costs.py keeps every digit; spread.py prints whole millionths, and the embedding is a fraction of one.

choices.text: No model is called
choices.why: Right. Nothing cleared the floor, so the request paid only for its embedding.

prompt: The 95th percentile cost of a help request is twice the median. Which setting drives that most?

choices.text: The model's maximum output tokens, which caps how long a reply can be
choices.why: The answers are short; the prompts are what vary.

choices.text: The temperature
choices.why: The assistant asks at temperature 0, and temperature does not change token counts much anyway.

choices.text: k and the floor, which decide how many sources go into the prompt
choices.why: Right. Three chunks in the prompt cost three times one, and nobody thinks of k as a price.

choices.text: The pseudonym key
choices.why: It has nothing to do with tokens.

prompt: Who were the two heaviest users of the week?

choices.text: The support team
choices.why: Right. The feature column said what they were without saying who.

choices.text: Two customers scripting the assistant against its API every night
choices.why: Their only feature was summary, which customers do not use.

choices.text: The replay itself, which counts as a user
choices.why: Each request carries its own user from the traffic file.

choices.text: Anonymous users, grouped under one hash
choices.why: Every replayed request has a user.

prompt: Why does the per-user table show the features each user touched?

choices.text: So the pseudonym can be reversed
choices.why: A list of features reverses nothing.

choices.text: Without it, the heaviest users looked like two customers to investigate
choices.why: Right. Who they are stays hidden; what they did is enough.

choices.text: Because cost per user cannot be computed without it
choices.why: The cost needs only the pseudonym.

choices.text: To spread the cost across features
choices.why: It distributes nothing; it labels.

prompt: The replayed week's per-user curve is flat. Why should a real one not be assumed flat?

choices.text: Real users always cost the same as each other
choices.why: That would make the real curve flat too.

choices.text: Pseudonyms hide the heavy users
choices.why: A pseudonym is stable; heavy users still add up under it.

choices.text: The simulated week picks who asks at random every time; real use concentrates
choices.why: Right. The flatness is a property of how the week was generated.

choices.text: Real providers bill per user
choices.why: They bill per token and per key.

prompt: The cost per 1,000 requests fell from 0.66 on Tuesday to 0.55 on Wednesday. What caused it?

choices.text: The new release raised the floor
choices.why: That was Thursday at 10:00.

choices.text: Fewer customers asked questions
choices.why: Wednesday had 45 requests, Tuesday 47; volume does not change cost per request anyway.

choices.text: The cache started working
choices.why: There is no cache in this assistant.

choices.text: The price cut of 30 September
choices.why: Right. The price per token fell 25%; tokens per request moved only with the day's noise.

prompt: Under release 2026.10.1, how many input tokens did a request carry on average (21,450 over 161)?
Which number separates a change in usage from a change in price?

choices.text: Tokens per request
choices.why: Right. No price list can move it.

choices.text: Cost per request
choices.why: It moves with both, and cannot say which.

choices.text: Total cost per day
choices.why: It moves with volume as well as price and usage.

choices.text: The share of each feature in the cost
choices.why: A price cut that applies to all models leaves shares unchanged and the bill lower.

prompt: Why is the fall in cost after Thursday's release not good news?

choices.text: Because the price went back up
choices.why: It did not.

choices.text: It got cheaper by answering less
choices.why: Right. Fewer sources passed the floor and more requests were refused.

choices.text: Because cost is meant to stay constant
choices.why: A fall is welcome when it comes from doing the same work for less.

choices.text: Because weekends are always cheaper
choices.why: Thursday itself fell, before the weekend, and per request, not in total.

prompt: The provider's invoice is ten percent higher than the sum of the spans. What is the likeliest explanation?

choices.text: Rounding in Decimal
choices.why: Decimal does not round away ten percent.

choices.text: The clock offset of the replay, which shifts every span by days
choices.why: The offset moves times, not tokens.

choices.text: The pseudonyms
choices.why: They change nothing about tokens.

choices.text: Work done with the key that no span recorded
choices.why: Right. A percent or two is noise; ten is untraced work.

prompt: A streamed reply was cut off half way. Why does its span have no usage, though the provider may still charge for it?

choices.text: The SDK deletes usage on errors
choices.why: There was never any usage to delete.

choices.text: Providers never charge for a streamed reply that did not finish
choices.why: They charge for tokens produced, streamed or not.

choices.text: Usage comes in the last chunk, which was lost
choices.why: Right. The span records the pieces received, not tokens.

choices.text: The redaction removed it
choices.why: Redaction touches text attributes, not counts.

prompt: Which of these can make the invoice differ from the sum of the spans? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A batch job using the same key without instrumentation
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Cached prompt tokens priced as ordinary input
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Exchange rates and taxes
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The trace ids being 32 characters long
choices.why: Ids have nothing to do with money.

prompt: Where does a per-user daily cap have to be checked to be useful?

choices.text: Before the next call
choices.why: Right, against a running total. The spans stay the record; the running total is the brake.

choices.text: In a report the next morning, compared with the previous day's
choices.why: By then the money is spent.

choices.text: Only in the provider's console
choices.why: That is the last line, not the first.

choices.text: In the tracing backend
choices.why: The backend sees spans after the call has been paid for.

prompt: Help and order stopped crossing their budgets from Wednesday on. What does the lesson say that means?

choices.text: The team got better at spending
choices.why: Nobody did anything to save money that week.

choices.text: The budgets were raised on Wednesday morning
choices.why: budgets.json was the same all week.

choices.text: The price cut, then the release
choices.why: Right. Not restraint.

choices.text: Weekends have no traffic
choices.why: Saturday and Sunday had 36 and 34 requests.

prompt: Match each view of the bill to the question it answers.

pairs.right: is this thing worth what it costs?
is one account spending what everybody else does?
did a change move the tokens per request?

right_distractors: which model is the most accurate?

prompt: A price that is a new row with a start date, keeping the old one for its days, is called ___-dated.
Put the steps of costs.py for one span in order.
items: read the model and the token counts off the span
find the day the span ran
look up the price in force that day
multiply and divide by a million
